messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Ethan was 29, a North American Jewish man who lived alone and worked as a jeweler in a small storefront district, the kind of job that required him to spend long hours bent over a counter under bright lights, handling tools and inspecting fine details. He had gone overseas as a relief worker into a war zone, telling people at the time that he could tolerate the chaos because he was useful there, because someone had to sort supplies, carry water, and help get children and families to safer ground. The day that changed him came when he was moving through a damaged school building that had been turned into a shelter. In the crush of bodies and shouting, he suddenly heard children crying from a back room, saw men carrying long metal objects that could have been tools or weapons, and felt an unexpected hand clamp onto his shoulder as someone tried to pull him aside. At the same instant, his own heart began pounding so hard that he could feel it in his throat. Since then, Ethan has said that even the smallest cue can drop him back into that moment without warning: the slam of a door near his apartment, a child wailing on the sidewalk, or the jolt of his pulse during an ordinary walk to work can bring the whole scene back with a force that feels immediate and overwhelming. He does not experience these memories as distant recollections. He describes them as more real than his everyday life, vivid in their sounds and bodily sensations, and at times he feels the emotional intensity of the event flood him without any clear image at all, as if terror arrives first and the picture follows, if it follows at all.

What has made those intrusions so hard to escape is the way Ethan now watches the world. Since returning home, he has been on constant alert for potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, and he cannot settle unless his back is against a wall where he can see the room. Even when friends or coworkers tell him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them. In his mind, safety is something other people can afford to assume, not something he is allowed to trust. That vigilance has made ordinary places feel full of hidden threat, and it also keeps the war zone memory close at hand, because every knife on a restaurant table, every heavy tool in the jewelry shop, every sudden movement near him seems to confirm that danger can appear anywhere. When he is scanning for threats, small physical sensations become loaded too. If his heart starts racing while he is leaning over a display case, he notices it instantly, and that pounding body sensation can pull the entire memory back into the room with him. Likewise, the sound of children crying outside the storefront or in the apartments above his shop can do the same. It does not matter that he knows he is in his own neighborhood; the fear in his body makes the past feel present.

Ethan has tried hard to manage this by talking himself down. He reminds himself that it could have been worse, that other people had it far worse, and he forces himself to think only positive thoughts when the images or feelings rise up. He tells himself to be grateful that he made it home, that he has work, that he is not in a bombed-out school anymore. But these efforts have not given him relief for long. Instead, they often seem to push the memory sideways rather than away, leaving him with the same violent emotional charge and, paradoxically, more scanning. When he tells himself to stay positive, he becomes even more determined not to look at what is wrong, and then the memory returns with its full force in some stray detail—a child’s cry, a shoulder brush from a stranger, his own pulse thudding in his chest. At those moments he begins checking the surroundings all over again, reading every corner of the room for danger, and the more he searches, the more dangerous the world appears. The shop has become especially difficult because he cannot control where customers stand or where their hands move, and an unexpected touch from behind the counter can make him jump hard enough that he has embarrassed himself in front of clients. Over time he has started choosing positions in the shop and in restaurants that let him keep his back protected, and he has cut short social outings because he cannot relax enough to stay.

The cost has been growing. Ethan has become quieter with friends, less willing to meet people after work, and increasingly isolated in his apartment, where he still finds himself scanning the rooms before he can sit down. His days are organized around not being startled, not being cornered, not hearing children cry if he can help it. He finally sought help after a morning in the shop when his heart began racing as a parent and child passed outside, the child crying against the glass while a customer touched his arm from behind to ask a question. The memory hit him so fully that he had to step into the back room and sit on the floor until he could breathe. He came to treatment afraid that his body and mind were no longer obeying him, and most afraid that he would keep living as if the war were still happening, unable to trust that he is truly home.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows cues bringing back the memory, but does not clearly state that triggers themselves cause or lead to the traumatic memory in the same-paragraph causal sense required.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette describes the memory leading Ethan to scan for cues, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself generates or activates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette portrays Ethan as perceiving the world as dangerous, but it does not explicitly connect that sense of threat to the traumatic memory coming back.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows that threat scanning happens alongside reminders of danger, but it does not clearly say that his sense of threat causes specific triggers/reminders to arise.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Ethan uses talking himself down and positive thinking, but the vignette does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies lead to the memory returning or being maintained.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette shows his coping efforts alongside later checking and scanning, but it does not clearly state that the maladaptive strategies themselves generate triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since then, Ethan has said that even the smallest cue can drop him back into that moment without warning: the slam of a door near his apartment, a child wailing on the sidewalk, or the jolt of his pulse during an ordinary walk to work can bring the whole scene back with a force that feels immediate and overwhelming. He does not experience these memories as distant recollections.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When one of those cues hits, it does not stay a cue for long; the sound or sensation itself seems to drag him straight back into the damaged school, and the memory arrives as if it is happening again rather than being remembered.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He describes them as more real than his everyday life, vivid in their sounds and bodily sensations, and at times he feels the emotional intensity of the event flood him without any clear image at all, as if terror arrives first and the picture follows, if it follows at all.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because the memory comes back so vividly, he starts noticing reminders everywhere — a child crying outside the storefront, a hard jolt in his chest, a stranger’s hand near his shoulder — and each one gets read as another sign that the event is close behind him.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since returning home, he has been on constant alert for potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, and he cannot settle unless his back is against a wall where he can see the room. Even when friends or coworkers tell him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of threat keeps the school memory active in his mind; the more dangerous the world feels, the more readily the scene returns, as though his body has to keep revisiting it to stay prepared for what might happen next.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That vigilance has made ordinary places feel full of hidden threat, and it also keeps the war zone memory close at hand, because every knife on a restaurant table, every heavy tool in the jewelry shop, every sudden movement near him seems to confirm that danger can appear anywhere.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he is in that threat state, almost anything can turn into a reminder — the metal edges of a ring tray, a customer shifting too quickly at the counter, a door opening behind him — and the world around him starts to look arranged around the event.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He tells himself to be grateful that he made it home, that he has work, that he is not in a bombed-out school anymore.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But the effort of pushing it away has not emptied it out; keeping himself from thinking about it has only left the memory intact and waiting, so that when his guard slips the scene comes back louder and more forceful than before.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
At those moments he begins checking the surroundings all over again, reading every corner of the room for danger, and the more he searches, the more dangerous the world appears.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The habits built out of trying to manage his fear have also drawn a map of reminders around him, so that every route he avoids in the neighborhood, every place he chooses not to stand in the shop, and every hand he keeps at arm’s length becomes its own signal that the attack still matters.
<<<END>>>
